chapter: Early life and Halfway House years
title: Early life, instruments, Halfway House bands, cabaret jobs and first recordings
summary: Cordilla gives his birth and family details, his lessons on trumpet then clarinet, the Rappolo clarinet story, the Halfway House band, early cabaret jobs, and the first records, ending on the New Orleans Rhythm Kings session.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: My name is Charlie Joseph Cadilla. I was born in Baton Rouge, May the 25th, 1899. Joe, is your middle name? Joseph. Charles Joseph. And when did you move to New Orleans? Oh, when I was about six years old. How many brothers and sisters did you have? Five boys and four girls. And they're all living still? All but one. Is that so? Were you the oldest or the youngest? No, I'm the youngest. The youngest? That's a pretty good record. How many kids you got of your own? None. Married how long? It'll be 27 years, December coming. The one woman? Yes. A good one, I know it too. How long can you remember being interested in music, Charlie? Oh, I'd say back in 1916, somewhere around that. So were you self-taught or did you take lessons? No, I took lessons. For how long? Oh, I'd say about two or three years. And what'd you start on? I started on... Four bitches on the violin. Was it? I started on trumpet. Trumpet, did you? Yeah. Trumpet. Did you play any of the percussion instruments? No. No play the guitar? No. No piano? No. No piano? No. Well, from trumpet you went? I jumped the clarinet. Right away? Yeah. What'd you have, an old Albert system? That's right. Still have it. You still have it? Still have the old Albert system. Weren't you from the original days? You still have it? No. Yes, from the halfway house. The clarinet that was... You got rubber bands all over it? Yeah. Maybe one or two of them. What kind of a sax do you play, Charlie? Tenor sax. Tenor? Yeah. What kind of a do you have? A busher. A busher? How many years you had in that? Oh, I'd say about 20 years. That's... When is the last official recording session that you were in? Do you remember that? Well, I think back in 1924, something like that. Is that so? Charlie, how do you spell your last name? There's been a lot of mistakes made about that in phonograph recording companies and write-ups about you that always change it. Would you spell your name correctly, the last name? C-O-R-D-I-L-L-A. Fine. Now, that's down for posterity forever and ever. What was your father's name? Anthony Cadilla. Any middle name, too? No. Anthony. Now, tell me some more about that Albert System clarinet. Well, I have an old con clarinet. Now, it was brand new when I got a hold of it by my real good clarinet. It was an old Pendle Muller. I purchased it when I was playing out at the halfway house. Rapolo, he used to come in and sit in with us and play my clarinet. He liked it. Wait a minute now. I'm going to stop you right there. That means that you were in the halfway house orchestra before Leon Rapolo joined. That's right. He used to sit in with you. That's right. I'm going to take it from there. And he used to like to play my clarinet very much. He liked it. Really liked it. It was an old Pendle Muller clarinet. Was he older or younger than you? I'd say about the same age. Self-talk, too? He took lessons. I think he took lessons. Tell me some more about that clarinet. Well, it just so happened that one night they met on Canal Street, Angelo Gimela, with that brand new con clarinet and Buzzy Willow's with his guitar. And I was walking out of the halfway house and they decided to go out to the lake and play a few tunes with Angelo's clarinet, Angelo Gimela's new clarinet. So they were out on their way to West End and they decided to stop at the halfway house. And it gave Leon an idea to get my clarinet because he loved to play it. And he stopped out there and asked me to let him have my clarinet to go out there and play a while. And I'd use Gimela's brand new con clarinet. Well, I was undecided about it at first. I didn't want to let him have it. So Angelo decided to make a deal with me. He said if anything would happen to my Pendle Muller clarinet, that he would let me have the brand new con clarinet. So that was okay. So they left me Angelo's clarinet and I gave rap my clarinet. They went out to the lake and they started to play a few tunes. And something happened. Somehow or another, he started missing a few licks on my clarinet. And he just got wool gathered and threw the clarinet over in the lake. Well, that was towards the end of his life? Well, that was the beginning. He was well-oriented and not excitable or anything? No, no. Was he always from the beginning excitable, boy? Yeah. He was, huh? Yeah. Now, Charlie, when you were at the old halfway house, I remember I'm a little bit older than you are, but I can remember that the music coming from out in that place was wonderful and it attracted customers. But we all had the idea that anybody who went in the halfway house was damned to perdition the rest of their life. And when I finally raked up enough nerve to go in, it was nothing doing but a lot of people sitting around and dancing. That's right, Doctor. Didn't they have sand on the floor in that place? Yeah. You remember that big old trellis in the back there? Yeah, that's right. Now, tell me who was in your group that you played with halfway house yourself first. Well, when we first started, we had Abby Burness. He was the leader of the band. Trumpet, myself on clarinet, and Stale Bread, Emil Lacombe on guitar. I was going to ask you about him. Was he blind at the time that you played with him? He was, yeah. Already, huh? Yes, Doctor. But didn't he play banjo, guitar, and piano? Yes. He did, huh? He did, huh? Not good, though, huh? Well, uh... Was he any good? Yeah, he played all right, Doctor. He did, huh? Yeah. By the way, it wasn't guitar. It was banjo. It was. Yeah. Uh-huh. Then we had Mickey Marco on piano, and Emmett Rogers on drums. That's Buck's brother, isn't it? That's right, yeah. Is he living still? Emmett, no, he died. By Stale Bread's dead, and... Emmett's dead. Emmett's dead. Now, what about Mickey Marco? He's living here. He's still living here. He lives across the river, doesn't he? That's it, yes. He lives over in Algeria. What's his brother clarinet player? I mean, the violin player. Well, Oscar. Oscar Marco, yeah. Now, let me ask you some more. Did you have drums? That was Rogers. That's right. And piano? Drums, piano. Who was it on? That's Mickey. Mickey? You had no trombone, huh? No trombone. No sax. Just you doubled on sax and sax? Well, later, yeah. Later, during the time that we were out there, the sax got popular, and I decided to get a saxophone. Ah. But we first started out there. Do you remember about what year that was? 1920 we started out there. Not before then, huh? Not before. Did you play any place professionally before then? Yes, I did, doctor. That would have made you around 23 years old then, wasn't it, when you started playing? That's right. Where did you play before then? Well, I played, uh, my first, uh, cabaret job was in old Pop Toro's Cabaret on Burgundy Street, Burgundy and Iverville. What was in there? The Toro's? Toro's Cabaret. Uh-huh. Pop Toro's. Well, that was after the old district was closed, though, wasn't it? Uh, that's right. That's right. That's right. Yeah, that's right. Did you ever play in the old district during the war? No, doctor. You mean before then? No, doctor. You didn't, doctor? No. Charlie, can you remember the personnel of the band, the Toro's? Uh, I, uh, I can think of, uh, one of, uh, maybe two or three of them, doctor. I can't remember the drummer's name. I can, uh, uh, they had, uh, uh, Georgia Brunus on trombone. Uh, and, uh, Eddie Shields on piano. And we had... And we had... And Larry's brother? That's right. And, uh, we had, uh, Stale Bread, Emile Lacombe on banjo. That was the setup there. I think they had, uh, four or five pieces there. Rapolo was playing there, but he quit. And, uh, I went on down there and got the job. I replaced, uh, Leon. Uh-huh. And, uh... Then from, uh, that, that Cabaret, where'd you go? From there, I went, uh, Rap, went to work out at Bucktown. Uh, they had a piano player out there by the name of Billy Neuberger. He was playing, I can't remember this. They had a violin player and they had drums, just a small combination. And they had Rap on clarinet out there. Well, Rap worked out there for, uh, oh, I'd say a month or so. And he quit there. And I left, uh, Pop Toros to go in his place out there. Did it seem like you would follow him? Yeah. That's right. And then from how long did you stay out there? Oh, I'd say about four or five months. And, uh, then I quit out there. Was it pretty rough out there, Charles? Oh, yeah. It was really rough. On Saturday night, there was brawls out there. Oh, yeah. Rough and tumble, of fact. That's that old cavalry up on stilts. You had to go up a long high step. Yeah, that's it. That's right. Yeah. And if you ever got boxed up in there, the fight started you in a bad figure. You, you said something there. You'd really come coming down the steps. Yeah, yeah. And then from there, where? Then from there, uh, I was out for a while. I have a picture you gave me, uh, of Stale Brad and Abby Brunis and you, and shirt sleeves taken out at, uh, West End. West End, yeah. Is that about the same time you were playing? That was when we were out at the halfway house. We used to go out there during the evenings and have our kicks out there. On your time off, you'd go play music. That's right. Now, tell me a little bit more. After you left Bucktown, you remember where you went? Well, no, I, uh, I was, uh, off for a while and, uh, Shockey was playing down at the old Taunty on a Saturday night and I joined him down there playing with him on a Saturday. He had a nice outfit down there. And, uh, right from there, I went to the halfway house. I remember that very well. And then, uh, tell me this, the first recordings that you ever made, were they under the heading of the halfway house? That's right, yeah. Yeah, what was the group, uh, who was in that group? Abby? Abby, uh, Mickey, Marco on piano, Emmett Rogers on drums, myself on clarinet, and, uh, Emile Lacombe on, uh, banjo. Now, the first two tunes, I believe I have the original record at home. Can you remember them? Yes, I think it was, uh, Pussycat Rag and, uh, Barataria. That was for the OK record. And, uh, Rap was on that one, too, wasn't he? That's right, yeah. And the, the one that followed after that was, uh, Rap was no longer with the group. That's right. And if I remember correctly, that was Let Me Call You Sweetheart. And what was the other side? Uh, Let Me Call You Sweetheart and Maple Leaf. That's right. That's right. And you, you have all the clarinet work on both of those. That's right, yeah. That was a fine group, and I think they'll remember you by that. Those two over anything else. You have some fine ones that went on for, uh, Columbia sessions that followed, didn't you? Yeah, exactly. Did you have two, three different sessions that came on after that? Yeah. For Columbia. Yeah. Those are fine discs. If you see them today, the surfaces are as good as they were, 25 years ago, John. Yes, sir. They compare with the, uh, the, uh, hi-fi relative recordings today, those old Columbia still stand up. That's marvelous. Someday I want you over to my house to hear your own self, how fine it came to you. Yeah, doctor. Uh, I, I'd say that I was, uh, pretty, I was out there for about five years on clarinet. That's one of the longest jobs you ever held, right? I think so, doctor. Uh, why'd they fold up? Business just got bad? Yeah. I left before they folded up, though. I went with, uh, Paul Merez. So that's what I was going to ask you to do. The next group that you record with was in your own rhythm king, right? That's right. A big, tall record, uh, we recorded. Uh, rap was supposed to play clarinet, and I was supposed to play tenor on that particular record, but somehow or another, the day before we recorded, we had a rehearsal, and, and they got into a, uh, rap and, uh, Santo Pecora got into some kind of an argument, and, and rap got hotheaded and decided to pack his clarinet up and leave. So I told Paul, uh, goodness sake, get him back here, man. We got a good, uh, deal coming on recording that record, and he had a very nice solo, and Paul said, no, he's hardhead, let him go. So he walked out. So Paul decided, uh, to have me to play clarinet. Uh-huh. And, and just disregard the tenor. Uh-huh. So we went up there the next morning to record that, uh. Where was that recording session held? Uh, I can't, uh, exactly remember. I think it was on Canal Street, one of the music houses. Was it a regular studio, or you just went into a room and then they set up the thing? Just, uh, a room and they set it up. That's right. Did they have, uh, microphones and all the things? Yes, Doctor, they had, uh, the voice came out with the microphone. So those were the, after the days of the old horn? The old horn, like the first one recorded was an OK record, I think, with the horn. How'd you have to record that? Well, each man threw a horn. Oh. Uh. No drums either, huh? No, they were pretty. They were just on wood blocks. Wood blocks, uh, cymbal. You know why, huh, Charlie? Oh, I guess. They would jump the needle off and see. Yeah.
